notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material from Guzik, Matthew Henry, Gill, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary, plus a sermon by John Piper and some notes on the early Church. I didn't reach netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, preceptaustin.org or any Lutheran, Methodist or Pentecostal-denomination site, so there's nothing from those below. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter.

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Ellicott says "cry aloud" literally means crying "with the throat": full voice, not soft words. Someone calling people to repent must not speak "smooth things," and the trumpet image makes the same point. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html
- Matthew Henry: the prophet must not hold back from probing the wound, even if it makes him unpopular. He adds that a trumpet is loud but clear, so the warning must be easy to understand. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_058.cfm

**v. 2:** The Pulpit Commentary compares this verse with Isaiah 1:11–15. It says these people were not deliberate hypocrites. Rather, they thought religion was outward observance and didn't see that it is the devotion of the heart. It gives two readings of "they ask me for righteous judgments": they want God to judge their enemies, or they want God to keep His side of the covenant as they think they have kept theirs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/58.htm
- Ellicott hears irony in every phrase: each mark of true devotion listed here is one the people did not actually have. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html
- Guzik calls this the *appearance* of their spiritual life. On the surface they seemed to love God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-58/
- Henry warns that "Men may go a great way towards heaven and yet come short". https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_058.cfm

**v. 3:** The Pulpit Commentary thinks the fast is probably the Day of Atonement, the only fast the Law commanded. The people expected a definite payoff and felt badly treated when none came. It reads "do as you please" as "carry on business" on a day meant to be free of work, and says holy days were meant to bring relief to the poor. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/58.htm
- Guzik: even on fast days they still exploited their employees. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-58/
- The Geneva Bible notes say the prophet exposes the hypocrites through "the second table and by their duty toward their neighbour". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/58-3.htm

**v. 4:** Ellicott suggests that fasting without real spiritual purpose can make people irritable and bad-tempered. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html
- The Pulpit Commentary gives two options: hunger made people quarrelsome (Delitzsch's view), or there were two parties, and one fasted to provoke the other. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/58.htm
- Guzik thinks they fasted for selfish requests, such as winning an argument. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-58/
- Henry: instead of judging themselves on the fast day, they blamed each other. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_058.cfm

**v. 5:** Ellicott: "afflict his soul" comes from Leviticus 16:29 and means the inner sorrow that was the true goal of fasting. The bowing "like a reed" is mechanical, like a bulrush swaying in the wind. He links this to Jesus saying John the Baptist was no "reed shaken by the wind." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html
- Guzik: God is not against fasting but against empty ritual. The answer is not to stop fasting but to get right with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-58/

**v. 6:** The Pulpit Commentary quotes Dr. Kay: the passage reads like a sermon for the Day of Atonement. It notes that Jews call the true fast "the fasting of the heart." It suggests the verse means freeing slaves, cancelling debts and returning pledges. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/58.htm
- Ellicott: the verse does not rule out going without food, but says it is not enough on its own. He notes that the "yoke" was fastened with leather straps, and contrasts the Pharisees, who loaded people with heavy burdens, with Christ, who lifted them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html
- Barnes: fasting is right, but the kind God approves leads to justice and charity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/58-6.html
- Guzik: getting right with God starts by stopping the wrong we do to others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-58/

**v. 7:** Ellicott: "share your bread" is literally "break bread." "Cast out" covers every kind of homelessness, including evicted tenants, runaway slaves and refugees. He links the verse with Matthew 25:35–36. "Your own flesh" first meant fellow Israelites, but it can extend to all suffering people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the early Christian saying that fasting and almsgiving are "the wings of prayer." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/58.htm

**v. 8:** Ellicott sees a pile of images: dawn, new flesh healing after a long illness, righteousness (being publicly cleared) leading the march, and God's glory guarding the rear. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html
- The Pulpit Commentary reads "healing" as recovery from the low state the people's sins had brought them to. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/58.htm
- Henry: good people are kept safe on every side. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_058.cfm

**v. 9:** Ellicott: pointing the finger is a near-universal sign of scorn, the action version of saying "Raca" or "You fool" (Matthew 5:22). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html
- Henry: if you shut your ears to the poor, God won't hear you; if you are generous, your prayers rise with your gifts, like Cornelius's (Acts 10:4). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_058.cfm
- Guzik reads the verse as three things to *stop* doing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-58/

**v. 10:** For "give yourself to the hungry" (literally "draw out your soul"), Ellicott weighs three meanings: giving up your own wants, sharing your goods, or extending sympathy. He prefers sympathy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html
- The Pulpit Commentary agrees: give compassion along with the bread. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/58.htm
- Guzik: failing here is a sin of omission. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-58/

**v. 11:** The Pulpit Commentary: "sun-scorched land" means times of spiritual low and weariness, and "strengthen your frame" means God keeps your strength up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/58.htm
- Gill compares God's guidance to the pillar of cloud and fire, and applies the "spring" to the life Christ gives inside each believer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/58.htm

**v. 12:** Ellicott: this mainly means rebuilding Jerusalem, but it has a wider spiritual application too. "Streets of dwelling" means streets lined with houses again. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html
- The Pulpit Commentary says the restoration covers customs as well as cities. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/58.htm
- Guzik: you can't build anything for God on a shallow faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-58/

**v. 13:** Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary both say "turn your foot" pictures the Sabbath as holy ground, and that "your pleasure" is better translated "your business." The Pulpit Commentary adds that the Sabbath needed both a deeper spirit and stricter keeping. What matters is the *kind* of words spoken on it, not how many. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/58.htm

**v. 14:** The Pulpit Commentary: worship becomes a real joy, and "the heritage of Jacob" points to the whole world being blessed through Jacob's seed. It says the Christian Church has inherited these promises. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/58.htm
- Ellicott reads "the heights of the land" as the land of Canaan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html

## Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 6, fasting itself:** Calvin (Reformed) notes that the prophet appears to abolish fasting universally when he lists works of mercy in its place. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/58-6.html
- Ellicott (Anglican) disagrees, saying the verse doesn't rule out fasting. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html
- An Anglican Ash Wednesday sermon (A. G. Mortimer) applies the chapter to Lent: fasting should go with repentance, almsgiving and prayer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/edt/isaiah-58.html

**vv. 1, 6–7, Gill's Baptist/Dissenter reading:** Gill applies the chapter to "the present reformed churches." He reads the "bands of wickedness" as rules imposed on conscience, such as set forms of prayer, and the "poor cast out" as ministers expelled from their churches. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/58.htm

**vv. 6–12, social justice:** John Piper (Baptist) says faith that doesn't produce "a passion for God-exalting social justice and practical mercy is worthless". He sets this alongside the need for faith, forgiveness and holiness. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/bethlehem-break-forth-like-the-dawn

**v. 13, the Sabbath (the clearest split):**
- Guzik says the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), so Christians are free to keep any day, or none, as a Sabbath. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-58/
- Gill (Baptist) and Matthew Henry (Presbyterian Nonconformist) teach strict keeping of the day as a delight: no worldly business, walks in the fields or worldly talk. Gill links the delight to remembering Christ's redemption. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/web/isaiah/58-13.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/58-13.html
- Calvin says the "delight" is God's, not ours. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/58-13.html
- A biblehub Q&A article (not tied to a named tradition) says Sunday worship keeps the principle, because Christ's resurrection begins a new creation. https://biblehub.com/q/isaiah_58_13__sabbath_vs._sunday_worship.htm

## Other views

**Date and setting (older critical debate; no modern scholarly site found):**
- Ellicott thinks the setting fits Manasseh's reign. He notes that those who date the book later point to the fasts set up after the exile (Zechariah 7–8). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-58.html
- The Pulpit Commentary sees Isaiah's own contemporaries. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/58.htm
- The Expositor's Bible weighs a setting among the exiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/isaiah/58.htm
- The Cambridge Bible sees "an incipient Pharisaism" in the people's hope that outward works would speed up salvation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/58-3.htm

**Early Church (in place of the Catholic and Orthodox sites I didn't reach):** The Letter of Barnabas quotes vv. 4–10. Justin Martyr cites vv. 6–7 to argue that God prefers justice to ritual, and urges Jews to keep "God's true fast." https://bible.org/seriespage/chapter-3-fasting-through-patristic-era
- The Pulpit Commentary also calls treating the bare act of fasting as spiritually effective (the *opus operatum*) a dangerous delusion. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/isaiah-58.html

**Popular modern teaching:** One biblehub article reads v. 8 against modern secular social-justice frameworks, arguing that justice must be rooted in worship. https://biblehub.com/q/Isaiah_58_8_s_impact_on_social_justice.htm
